newsitem.title: CHINA: China says HK to have freedom of speech inside law.
newsitem.headline: China says HK to have freedom of speech inside law.

text.p: China said on Thursday that Hong Kong people would have full freedom of expression after the British colony reverts to Beijing rule in 1997, but they should not attack Chinese internal affairs.

"Hong Kong should not interfere in mainland China's affairs by organising some political activities to attack the mainland's internal affairs," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a briefing on Thursday.
Hong Kong residents would have freedom of the press and freedom of speech but such liberities would have to operate within the boundaries of the law, Shen said.
"Hong Kong people will have full freedom of expression, but all freedoms must be within the limits allowed by law," Shen said.

He had been asked whether Hong Kong residents would be allowed to hold ceremonies to commemorate Beijing's bloody June 4, 1989 crackdown on students demonstrating for more democracy in Tiananmen Square.
"Any activities held in Hong Kong must be in accordance with legal regulations," he said.
Shen said the territory, a British colony for a century and a half, would maintain its capitalist system after it returns to mainland control at midnight on June 30, 1997.
"There will be no changes to our one country, two systems policy, the Hong Kong people will rule Hong Kong," Shen said.
Many Hong Kong residents have voiced fears the colony's lively media will be silenced by Beijing following the handover.
In an interview with the Asian Wall Street Journal published on Wednesday, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen warned of limits to freedom of speech.
The media "can put forward criticism, but not rumours or lies", the Journal quoted him as saying. "Nor can they put forward personal attacks on the Chinese leaders."
Shen said Qian's remarks marked no shift in Chinese policy on how it would handle Hong Kong after the handover.
